content_voiceover: Think of hemostasis as a seesaw between clot formation and clot breakdown. On the coagulation side, platelets and plasma clotting factors drive fibrin formation, but they're kept in check by a set of natural inhibitors: tissue factor pathway inhibitor, protein C, antithrombin, and heparin cofactor two. On the other side, fibrinolysis is driven by activators like tissue plasminogen activator and urokinase-type plasminogen activator, which convert plasminogen to plasmin to break down fibrin, and this too is restrained by inhibitors, mainly plasminogen activator inhibitor and alpha two antiplasmin. For boards, the key concept is that thrombosis and bleeding both result from tipping this balance, either too much drive or too little inhibition on either side. Memorize which inhibitors go with which pathway, since questions often test antithrombin deficiency or protein C deficiency as procoagulant states, versus excess alpha two antiplasmin or PAI-1 activity as antifibrinolytic states.
keypoints: Coagulation driven by platelets + plasma factors
Coagulation inhibited by TFPI, Protein C, antithrombin, heparin cofactor II
Fibrinolysis driven by t-PA and u-PA
Fibrinolysis inhibited by PAI-1 and alpha-2-antiplasmin
Disease = imbalance toward clotting or bleeding
keypoint_voiceover: Quick recap: coagulation is pushed by platelets and plasma factors, and held back by TFPI, protein C, antithrombin, and heparin cofactor two. Fibrinolysis is pushed by t-PA and u-PA, and held back by PAI-1 and alpha two antiplasmin. Disease states reflect an imbalance toward either clotting or bleeding.
